identification.basis: The dictionary gives kalka 'spear' and balur 'spear thrower'. Roth (1909) recorded kalka as the Koko-yellanji word for spear, and 'ballur' as the Bloomfield River name of the moon-shaped spear-thrower. Museums Victoria holds a Bloomfield River example catalogued under the local name Ballur.

summary: **Kalka** is the spear, and especially the fishing spear. **Balur**, **Milbayarr** and **mirrba** are the woomera, the spear-thrower whose hook, **mingu**, fits into the end of the spear [ref:hershberger1982]. Bloomfield River spears were built in two pieces: a light butt of [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree), reed or bamboo, and a hard tip of [black palm](entry:black-palm) (**duwar**), wattle or bloodwood, set with wooden or stingray barbs and sealed with tree gums [ref:roth1909] [ref:roth1904]. The Bloomfield people also made a curved, moon-shaped woomera, the *ballur*, which was known nowhere else. It was used for spearing fish and birds at close quarters and held in a grip of its own [ref:roth1909] [ref:mv].

sections.heading: Names
sections.body:
**Kalka** is 'fishing spear, also generic term for spear' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth found the same word for spear at Princess Charlotte Bay, Cape Bedford, the Bloomfield and the middle Palmer [ref:roth1909]. Fishing spears are also **yinba**, **yirrmba** ('many-pronged fish spear') and **jindal** ('spear with three prongs') [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth's Bloomfield *yirmbua*, a many-pronged fish spear, is the same word as yirrmba in his 1909 spelling [ref:roth1909]. Barbs are **jinil** or **manbir**. A [turtle](entry:sea-turtle)-spear point is **kurajan** in Yalanji and **biyul** in Nyungkul [ref:hershberger1982]. **Dara** and **wulburr** are bamboo spear sticks, and **duwar** is both the [black palm](entry:black-palm) and a spear made from it [ref:hershberger1982].

The woomera is **balur**, **Milbayarr** or **mirrba**. Its hook is **mingu**, and its decorated butt is **ngurmu** [ref:hershberger1982]. **Mumal** is 'to throw a spear with a woomera', and **damal** is 'to spear' [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: Description
sections.body:
**Spears.** Roth treated the spears of Princess Charlotte Bay, Cape Bedford, the Bloomfield and the middle Palmer as one family. Each is a light **butt** mortised onto a hard **tip**, and the end of the barb forms the very point of the spear [ref:roth1909]. The Bloomfield kinds he recorded, with his 1909 spellings, were [ref:roth1909]:

- ***do-war***: a reed butt with a short **[black-palm](entry:black-palm)** tip, which gives the spear its name. This is **duwar**, the 'black palm spear' of the dictionary [ref:hershberger1982].
- ***wur-poi***: a long [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree) butt with a short wattle (*Acacia holocarpa*) tip and a wooden barb.
- ***yirmbua***: a many-pronged fish spear of light wood, preferably grass-tree. People said it had first come from elsewhere, but it was being made on the Bloomfield before 1885.
- ***ta-chal*** and ***dikara***: fighting spears with a short grass-tree butt and a long black-palm or bloodwood shaft, carrying one stingray barb or several set one behind the other. ***ku-yan***: a fighting spear tipped with small [quartz](entry:stone) flakes set in gum. These are **dajal**, **dikarra** ('war spear, has a stingray barb') and **kuyan** ('war spear with quartz head') in the dictionary [ref:hershberger1982]. The heavy shovel-headed **murrangkal** of black palm is also a fighting spear [ref:hershberger1982].

**Woomeras.** At Cape Bedford, on the Endeavour and Bloomfield rivers and at Butcher's Hill, the ordinary spear-thrower was of **[ironwood](entry:ironwood)**. It had a long blade of even width and a short peg with a slight nick to take the spear butt. The peg was tied on with tendon through two drilled holes and covered with gum cement [ref:roth1909]. The handle was plain, or hafted with two pieces of baler shell (*Melo*) fixed with [beeswax](entry:native-bees), or with a thin lath bent back on itself [ref:roth1909].

The **ballur** of the Bloomfield, and of the short coast from there south to Cape Grafton, is different. It is bent like a new moon, short, light and without a haft, and usually [painted red](entry:red-ochre) and white at the far end [ref:roth1909]. The Museums Victoria example from the Bloomfield River (X 94769) is 790 mm long and 180 mm wide. It is curved, with a wooden peg bound at an acute angle and a rounded handle end. The museum notes that boomerang-shaped spear-throwers are known only from the Bloomfield area, and that Roth collected fourteen of them in 1898 [ref:mv].

sections.heading: Where the materials come from
sections.body:
- **[Black palm](entry:black-palm)** (*Normanbya normanbyi*, Roth's *Drymophloeus normanbyi*): on the Bloomfield its buds and young leaf-stalks were eaten, and its timber made spears. Roth's Bloomfield name is *du-ar*, the dictionary's **duwar** [ref:roth1901] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Bamboo and reed** for light butts: **dara**, **wulburr** [ref:hershberger1982].
- **[Grass-tree](entry:grass-tree)** (*Xanthorrhoea*) for butts and fish-spear prongs; its resin is **kanunjul** [ref:roth1909] [ref:hershberger1982].
- **[Ironwood](entry:ironwood)** (Cooktown ironwood, *Erythrophleum chlorostachys*) for woomeras, pegs and root gum. It grows in open forest and on rainforest margins across Cape York and north-east Queensland [ref:ironwood].
- **Woomera timbers** named in the dictionary: **ngadil**, 'hickory, good timber for woomeras', and **jinajina**, the water gum, 'good timber for woomeras' in the Yalanji dialect [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth saw Butcher's Hill woomeras made of a yellow timber he called *nga-til*, almost certainly the same word as ngadil [ref:roth1909].
- **Durral**: a tree whose wood is used for spears [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Wattle** for turtle-spear points: **kurrajan** is 'a spear point made from wattle' [ref:hershberger1982].
- **Stingray barbs**, from the coast. On the middle Palmer, inland, they were traded in from the Musgrave River on the east coast and from down the Mitchell [ref:roth1909].

For Western Yalanji country, Roth's records from the Koko-minni of the middle Palmer, Laura and Maytown are the nearest. There, spear-throwers were of ironwood with a long Acacia peg, nicked to take the spear butt and lashed with tendon under *Grevillea* cement. The haft was baler shell traded from the coast or a doubled lath of wood [ref:roth1909]. Their fish-spear butts were of bamboo bartered from Princess Charlotte Bay, with bone barbs [ref:roth1909].

sections.heading: Uses
sections.body:
**Fishing.** Kalka is first of all a fishing spear [ref:hershberger1982]. In deep or muddy waterholes where the fish could not be seen, men struck here and there on the chance of a hit, and every now and then they succeeded [ref:roth1901]. Roth often watched this at Princess Charlotte Bay [ref:roth1909]. Muddying a shallow pool with the feet and spearing the fish as they came up was common everywhere [ref:roth1901]. On the lower Tully, men waded in up to the waist after [eels](entry:eels) and jabbed single-pointed spears straight down among the leaves and water-grass. Pronged spears clogged in the tussocks [ref:roth1901].

**Birds and close work.** The Bloomfield ballur was used for spearing fish or birds, especially at very close quarters [ref:roth1909].

**Turtle.** **Kukuni** is 'the big spear used for spearing [turtle](entry:sea-turtle), used as a harpoon', and **kurrajan** is its fire-hardened wattle point [ref:hershberger1982].

**Fighting.** Spears were also weapons, and **damaway** is 'fight with spears' [ref:hershberger1982]. The war spears are listed above. The dictionary notes that the woomera also served as a shield to ward off spears [ref:hershberger1982].

sections.heading: How spears and woomeras were made and thrown
sections.body:
**Making a two-piece spear** (Bloomfield materials from Roth [ref:roth1909], methods from Roth [ref:roth1904]):

1. **Cut the parts.** Take a long, light butt of [grass-tree](entry:grass-tree), reed or bamboo, and a hard tip of [black palm](entry:black-palm), wattle or bloodwood.
2. **Straighten and harden.** Work the wood with heat. Charring in the fire hardens a point [ref:roth1904]. The dictionary word **balnji** covers doing a job 'properly with a fire as in cooking or hardening spears over a fire' [ref:hershberger1982].
3. **Cut the mortise.** Pick out the end of the butt with a hardened stick or bone awl. Lay red-hot cinders in the hole, blow on them, clear them out and pick again until the socket is deep enough [ref:roth1904].
4. **Fit the barb.** Bind on a wooden barb so that its end forms the very point. For fighting spears, a stingray barb was used instead [ref:roth1909].
5. **Bind it.** Lash the joints with [twine](entry:string-and-twine) or tendon. **Biyal** is sinew or string, especially [wallaby](entry:wallaby)-tail sinew [ref:hershberger1982].
6. **Seal the binding with gum.** Bloomfield gums [ref:roth1904]:
   - **Grass-tree resin** (**kanunjul**; Roth's KYE *kannojó-ol*). It lies in lumps among the roots and only needs heating [ref:roth1904] [ref:hershberger1982].
   - **Canarium gum**, from the 'brown cedar' (Roth's KYE *t-chaln-ji*; compare dictionary **jalnji**, a tree whose gum is used for making spears). Bake the dry lumps in leaves or warm them by the fire. Pound them between two greased [stones](entry:stone) until soft, then use the gum to fix haft and shaft together.
   - **[Ironwood](entry:ironwood) gum**, once made on the Bloomfield. Clear the roots of a young tree. Test a root by rubbing a [fire-stick](entry:firestick) on it and trying the melted gum between your teeth. If it is sticky, cut pieces off, strip the sticky covering, then roast and hammer it in turns until soft.
   - **Yikari**: in the dictionary, [beeswax](entry:native-bees) hardened with ironwood root juice and used to make spears [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth gave *yikari* as the Bloomfield name of a traded *Canarium muelleri* resin [ref:roth1904].
7. **Paint it.** On the Bloomfield, [ochre](entry:red-ochre) for spear-painting was fixed with [candlenut](entry:candlenut) oil [ref:roth1904].

**Making a woomera** (Cape Bedford–Bloomfield–Butcher's Hill type [ref:roth1909]):

1. Shape a long, even-width blade of ironwood, or of ngadil or jinajina [ref:hershberger1982].
2. Smooth it with the rough leaves of the sandpaper [fig](entry:fig) (*Ficus opposita*), as was done on the Bloomfield and the Laura [ref:roth1904].
3. Cut a short peg from *Petalostigma* with a slight nick in it. Lash it with tendon through two holes drilled in the blade, and cover the back with ironwood or, better, *Grevillea* cement [ref:roth1909].
4. Leave the handle plain, or fix on two pieces of baler shell with beeswax [ref:roth1909].

**Throwing** (**mumal**):

1. Fit the **mingu**, the hook, into the end of the spear butt [ref:hershberger1982].
2. For the ordinary woomera, the blade rests between the first and second fingers. For the Bloomfield ballur, it rests in the fork between the first finger and the thumb [ref:roth1909].
3. Throw. The woomera is 'a wooden instrument to help throw spears more powerfully' [ref:hershberger1982]. Roth describes the grips but not the rest of the throwing action, which is best learned from someone who still throws.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body:
A spear thrown with a woomera can kill. Throw only where you can see the whole field, never toward people, dogs or a camp, and walk to collect spears only when everyone has finished throwing. Spears glance. The dictionary has a word, **dalbarril**, for a spear bouncing off a [sea turtle](entry:sea-turtle)'s shell [ref:hershberger1982]. Barbed and stingray-tipped points tear on the way out.

Some traditional materials are hazardous. **Kulbawurr**, the resin gum of the cypress pine, is poisonous. It was used on spears in the old days, with an effect lasting about two hours [ref:hershberger1982]. [Ironwood](entry:ironwood) timber can cause dermatitis, and its splinters can cause complications [ref:ironwood]. Roasting and hammering gums means working close to fire and hot stones. Never carry a spear point-forward through camp.

sections.heading: On Country today
sections.body:
Under Queensland's *Fisheries Act 1994*, traditional fishing applies when the catch is for a personal, domestic or non-commercial communal need, follows the traditional laws and customs of the native title holders or Traditional Owners of the area, and is done by people with a connection to that land or water [ref:qldfish]. Section 211 of the *Native Title Act 1993* gives the same protection against licence and permit requirements for native title holders' hunting and fishing [ref:alrc]. Other people spearfishing must follow the ordinary fisheries rules.

Much Eastern Kuku Yalanji country, including the Daintree, Ngalba-bulal, Kalkajaka and Hope Islands national parks, is now Aboriginal land jointly managed with QPWS [ref:nit2021]. On Western Yalanji country the 2026 determination recognised rights to hunt, fish and gather over most of the area [ref:nit2026]. Visitors need the Traditional Owners' permission. Old spears and spear-throwers from the Bloomfield are held in museums, including the ballur at Museums Victoria [ref:mv].

sections.heading: Language
sections.body: **Damal** 'to spear'; **mungkil** 'spear to kill'; **ngura-ngura ngal** 'straighten, measure, aim'; **kajal** 'to tie'; **janbangal** 'to glue or stick something, using pitch or glue (yalanji only)' [ref:hershberger1982].
